faqs.q: Otters keep appearing in our Orlando lake — are they a problem?
faqs.a: They are a sign of a healthy lake chain and usually a delight, not a problem. River otters travel Orlando's connected lakes and canals, fish the shallows, and occasionally raid an unsecured dock box or a koi pond — the one genuine conflict, solved by securing the pond's fish with covers and removing fish-cleaning waste. Otters denning under a boathouse can be addressed under the nuisance rule; otters passing through need nothing but an audience. We will tell you which you have after a look at the sign.

Orlando.wildlife_intro:
Orlando's wildlife map is its lakes — hundreds of them, chained and scattered through every neighborhood from College Park's bungalows to Conway's shores to the downtown towers. Lake life means Muscovy ducks at every retention pond, raccoons in the canopy neighborhoods, roof rats in the palms, bats in the older commercial buildings, and otters commuting between lakes through the storm drains, to residents' regular astonishment. The eastern sprawl toward UCF and the northern suburbs toward Winter Park add subdivisions by the dozen.

Downtown and historic districts get building-scale work — bat colonies, pigeon systems — while the neighborhoods get house-scale exclusion and the lake communities get pond-duck counsel under the Control Order: control on property is lawful, release never is, feeding is the root problem. Our Orlando inspections are neighborhood-specific because Orlando is fifty neighborhoods wearing one name. Call (844) 544-3498 and tell us your lake or your district; the inspection follows the geography.

faqs.q: Peacocks roam our Winter Park street — what is the actual rule?
faqs.a: Peafowl in Winter Park are governed by local ordinance and long civic custom — the city has a known peacock population centered on its older neighborhoods, and what may be done about nuisance birds runs through city rules, not a trapper's preference. Feeding them concentrates the problem and is the first habit to stop. Protect car finishes in mating season, when males spar with their reflections. For a specific flock conflict, start with the city's guidance; we will map the ordinance honestly and handle any structure-entry issues — birds in an attic void are a different, excludable problem.

faqs.q: Rats are nesting in our Apopka nursery's stock — what is the approach?
faqs.a: Deny harborage and seal the structures. Nursery rats live in the stock itself — dense foliage on benches is cover — so the program pairs nonchemical trapping with bench spacing, debris and cull-pile discipline, and sealing the head houses and packing sheds where feed and supplies concentrate. Chemical programs are the Chapter 482 trade's. A nursery that runs clean aisles and sealed structures sees rat sign collapse; one that only traps harvests rats forever, and we quote the structural version.

faqs.q: Why are roof rats such a problem in Ocoee?
faqs.a: Roof rats are Florida's main structure rat, and Ocoee gives them exactly what they want: palm crowns, fruit trees, dense shrubs, and rooflines they can reach from fences and branches. They nest in attics and wall voids and breed year-round here. Our crew traps and excludes — sealing the entry and cutting back roof access — and frames structure work as nonchemical trapping and exclusion, because chemical rodent work in a structure is FDACS Chapter 482 pest-control territory.

Ocoee.wildlife_intro:
In Ocoee, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — dense urban and suburban Orlando, lake chains everywhere, and tourism corridors — and features such as Lake Apopka, Wekiwa Springs State Park, Econlockhatchee River, Lake Conway chain keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Ocoee jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: Our Horizon West home is brand new — why are we hearing attic noises?
faqs.a: Because new villages stand in old habitat. Horizon West rose from groves and pasture that held roof rats, raccoons, and squirrels the week before framing; the animals did not leave, they moved in — through the standard builder gaps every production roofline has. The noises are most often roof rats in the first year. A gap audit finds the pattern, trapping clears the pioneers, and sealing the roofline ends it. It is the most common call in every new Central Florida village, and the most fixable.

faqs.q: When can bats be excluded from a Maitland home?
faqs.a: Bat exclusion is legal in Florida from August 15 through April 15. Excluding or blocking bats during maternity season, April 16 through August 14, is illegal under FWC Rule 68A-9.010. The house bats here are Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats. In maternity season our crew can inspect, identify the roost, and schedule the exclusion for the legal window — and a bat found in a room with a sleeping person is a county health department call first.

faqs.a: Windermere quotes are estate-system figures: all structures on the property inspected and written as one scope with photo documentation, priced for the finish standard the town expects.

faqs.q: Otters have moved under our Windermere boathouse — what happens?
faqs.a: We confirm and evict by exclusion. A denning otter family under a boathouse is lawful nuisance work with your authorization: one-way exits or trapping, confirmation the space is empty, then sealing the under-boathouse voids so the next family chooses a bank instead. Otters merely fishing your dock are the chain working as designed. The Butler Chain's otters are strong swimmers and wide roamers — exclusion lasts because the boathouse stops being the best den on the shoreline, not because the otters left the lake.

Windermere is the Town Among the Lakes — a small, canopy-draped municipality on the Butler Chain, with dirt side streets, historic cottages, and some of Central Florida's most valuable lakefront behind its gates. The wildlife is lake-chain wildlife at estate scale: raccoons on the docks, roof rats in the palms, otters in the canals between lakes, and bats in the older cottages. Isleworth and the gated enclaves nearby extend the pattern.

Windermere work is discreet and thorough: estate inspections cover main house, boathouse, dock, and guest structures as one system, documented for owners and estate managers. The town's canopy and lake edges mean pressure is constant and gentle; the answer is a complete seal executed to an invisible standard. Otters get the resident-versus-tourist assessment, and the chain's gators, when one concerns a dock owner, get the FWC referral with the size-and-behavior facts.
